title: Tests
text:
Unless otherwise noted

Tests are closed book, but you may use four letter-sized sheets (both sides) of notes (eight sheets for the in-class portion of the final); notes must be handwritten or typed as you please; no sharing of notes during the test.
Calculators and other electronic devices are not allowed; phones must be placed in your bags under your desks or at the front of the room; hands must be on top of your desks.
You are expected to simplify any expressions that can be simplified as even numbers, but you may leave other expressions as is, e.g., \(\sqrt{47}\) or \(18/29\).
You will be provided all of the critical values that you need and are not expected to memorize them, but you should know how to use them.
Show all your work to justify your answers; answers without adequate justification will not receive credit.
You will be asked to sign an integrity statement on the question paper, and you are expected to abide by it.

title: Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling
text: The course project is an opportunity to investigate a topic in Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo methods and communicate its value clearly and critically. Approach the presentation as a report to colleagues who need to decide whether the article, method, or software feature is worth pursuing further.

title: Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling
text:
Project types
Choose one of the following project types.

Research article review: Review a scholarly research article related to Monte Carlo methods or their applications. This is an individual project, and each student must choose a different article. The topic should not substantially duplicate material discussed in class. In general, the article should have been published at least fifteen years ago.
QMCPy feature: Create a new feature for qmcpy and a blog post that illustrates it. This project may be completed individually or by a team of two. Discuss the proposed feature with the instructor to ensure that its scope is appropriate.

title: Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling
text:
Topic selection and approval

Choose a project type and identify a focused topic.
Submit the topic for approval. Revised topics will use the same process.
Check the approved-topic list after submissions have been reviewed and revise the proposal if requested.

For an article review, identify the main idea, illustrate it with examples of your own, offer warranted criticism, and suggest future work. For a QMCPy feature, explain the need for the feature, demonstrate its use, and discuss its strengths, limitations, and possible extensions.

title: Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling
text:
Presentation expectations

Prepare a 15-minute oral presentation followed by 5 minutes for questions and answers.
A two-person QMCPy feature team will have 30 minutes for the presentation followed by 10 minutes for questions and answers.
Prepare a handout for the audience.
Provide enough background for classmates who are not specialists in the exact topic, while remaining responsible for the technical details.
Explain both strengths and weaknesses, including important assumptions and limitations.
Be prepared to answer probing questions. Assessment depends on both the clarity of the presentation and the quality of the answers.

Detailed feedback questions and assessment guidance are on the Project Assessment page.

title: Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling
text:
Presentation guidance

Keep the big picture in view rather than getting bogged down in details.
Motivate the topic with relevant background, prior work, or applications.
Use a simple example to illuminate the main point.
Discuss strengths, weaknesses, alternatives, and possible future work.
Use clear plots, tables, pictures, and key formulas where they help the audience.
Use your own words and give appropriate credit; do not plagiarize.
Aim for roughly one slide per minute and avoid overloading slides.
Look at the audience rather than reading notes.
Practice beforehand, obtain feedback, and stay within the allotted time.
Review the Project Assessment questions while preparing the presentation.

title: Jupyter Notebooks

The course notebooks provide executable examples of Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo concepts, algorithms, applications, and computational performance. They are intended to complement the lectures and give students code that can be explored and adapted.
Notebooks will be organized by topic. Links will be added after each notebook has been migrated to the Fall 2026 repository, updated for the current course environment, and validated from a clean setup.

title: Jupyter Notebooks
text:
Sampling
Notebooks on random and low discrepancy sample generation, acceptance-rejection sampling, conditional Monte Carlo, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and related sampling methods will appear here.

Generating Samples — construct and transform IID and low discrepancy samples, including binomial, zero-inflated exponential, Gaussian-process, Brownian-motion, and financial-option examples

title: Jupyter Notebooks

Are We There Yet? — use a travel-time model to explore Monte Carlo convergence, error assessment, quantiles, conditional Monte Carlo, and randomized Sobol sampling

Additional notebooks will apply Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo methods to integration, financial options, queueing models, and other examples.

title: Welcome to MATH 565
text:
Course Description
This course teaches Monte Carlo simulation techniques, focusing on applications in financial risk management, uncertainty quantification, and Bayesian inference. These sampling methods are used to compute expected values, quantiles, and densities. Advanced techniques, including quasi-Monte Carlo and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, are covered. Students will gain experience using popular programming languages for Monte Carlo computations.


Instructor: Fred J. Hickernell



Office: Galvin Tower 18C3-1
Office hours: By appointment (book here)
Phone: 312-567-8983
Email: hickernell@illinoistech.edu
Website     LinkedIn     Google Scholar     Mathematics Genealogy Profile

Brief bio: Fred J. Hickernell is professor of applied mathematics. His research focuses on improving the efficiency of computer simulations and developing justifiable stopping criteria. He has spent most of his career at Hong Kong Baptist University and Illinois Institute of Technology, often in academic administrative roles. He has served on the editorial boards of the Journal of Complexity, Mathematics of Computation, and the SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis. He is a Fellow of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics and the recipient of the 2016 Joseph F. Traub Prize for Achievement in Information-Based Complexity.
Hickernell speaks Cantonese and enjoys Chinese food. He is married with adult children. He enjoys discussing matters of substance. His most important identity is a disciple of Jesus.

title: Big Statistics Questions We Ask
text:
Filter by course

  
     MATH 476 Statistics
     MATH 563 Mathematical Statistics
     MATH 565 Monte Carlo Methods
  
  



Modeling

  Course(s)
  Big question



  476, 563, 565
  
    What is the population?
    All US adults? All future units from a production line? All students with bachelor's degree? All continuous functions on a given domain?
  



  476, 563, 565
  
    What features are we interested in?
    Mean? Variance? Quantiles? Regression function? Entire distribution?
  



  476, 563
  
    What does the model fail to capture?
    Explanatory variables? Interactions? Nonlinearities?
  



  476, 563
  
    Are the distributional assumptions correct?
    Normality? Skewness? Heavy tails? Independence?
  



Sampling

  Course(s)
  Big question



  476, 563, 565
  
    How do we sample from the population?
    Independent and identically distributed (IID)? Low discrepancy (LD)? Stratified sampling? Designed experiment?
  



  476, 563
  
    What can go wrong between intended and actual sampling?
    Nonresponse and missingness? Measurement error? Coverage error?
  



Point Estimation

  Course(s)
  Big question



  476, 563
  
    What is the estimand?
    
      Parameter vs functional of a distribution
      What does it mean in context?
      What is random, what is fixed?
    
  



  563
  
    What makes an estimator “optimal”?
    
      Loss functions and risk
      Invariance/equivariance (as appropriate)
      Benchmarks and lower bounds (when assumptions hold)

title: Interesting Articles & Links
text:
This page collects optional articles, essays, videos, and interactive resources that connect probability, statistics, and data science to real applications, historical context, or broader ideas.

Statistical Inference and Data Science

The Lady Tasting Tea

A famous experiment conducted by Ronald Fisher to test whether a woman could distinguish between tea poured before or after milk
This experiment is often cited as an example of a randomized controlled trial and the basis for Fisher’s exact test

Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures

An influential paper by Leo Breiman that discusses the differences between traditional statistical modeling and algorithmic modeling in data science
Breiman argues that the algorithmic modeling culture, which focuses on predictive accuracy, is often more effective than the traditional statistical modeling culture, which focuses on inference and understanding

As Forecasts Go, You Can Bet on Monte Carlo

An article from the Wall Street Journal that discusses the use of Monte Carlo simulations in financial forecasting and risk management
The article highlights how Monte Carlo methods can help quantify uncertainty and improve decision-making in finance




Software and Libraries

qmcpy.org: A Python Library for Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods

A Python library for quasi-Monte Carlo methods, which are used to improve the efficiency of numerical integration and simulation

Rankings of Computer Languages

A ranking of programming languages based on their popularity and usage in the industry
Statistical questions include: What are the errors in the percentages? What is the significance of a change in rank?

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
text: This course uses a Git repository that includes submodules (shared libraries pulled in as separate Git repositories). To get everything working, you must clone the course repository and initialize the submodules.

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: Important: do not push to the course repository
text:
Important: do not push to the course repository
Students should assume the course repository is read-only:

Do not try to push changes to the course repository.
If you see errors like “permission denied” when pushing, that is expected.

You will not submit homework via Git. Git is used only to:

Obtain and update course materials
Experiment with class notebooks

When experimenting, consider working in copies of notebooks or in a separate directory so updates pull cleanly


If you want an online backup of your personal work, you may optionally use your own private repository or a fork (see below).

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
text:
Step 0: Prerequisites
You need:

Git installed
A way to authenticate with GitHub (either SSH or HTTPS)

Your instructor will provide the course repository URL. It looks like one of these:

SSH: git@github.com:ORG/MATHXXXSpring20YY.git
HTTPS: https://github.com/ORG/MATHXXXSpring20YY.git

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: Step 1: Clone the course repository with submodules
text:
Step 1: Clone the course repository with submodules
Choose one of the following.

Option A (recommended): clone with submodules in one step
Replace REPO_URL with the URL you were given.
git clone --recurse-submodules REPO_URL


Option B: clone first, then fetch submodules
git clone REPO_URL
cd MATHXXXSpring20YY
git submodule update --init --recursive

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: Step 2: Verify you have the submodule content
text:
Step 2: Verify you have the submodule content
From inside the course repository:
git submodule status
You should see one or more lines showing submodules and commit hashes. If you see errors or blank output, run:
git submodule update --init --recursive

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: Keeping your local copy updated during the semester
text:
Keeping your local copy updated during the semester
Do this whenever your instructor says “pull the latest changes.”
From inside the course repository:
git pull --ff-only
git submodule update --init --recursive
That second command is important: it updates submodules to the versions pinned by the course repository.

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: If you already made local changes
text:
If you already made local changes
If git pull --ff-only fails, it usually means you have local commits or uncommitted changes.
Check what changed:
git status

If you only changed files you don’t care about (quick reset)
git reset --hard
git pull --ff-only
git submodule update --init --recursive


If you want to keep your work
Commit your changes first so they are safely recorded locally.
git add -A
git commit -m "My work"
git pull --ff-only
git submodule update --init --recursive
If the pull still fails, you may need to resolve a merge conflict (ask for help).

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
section: Optional: fork workflow (push only to your own fork)
text:
Optional: fork workflow (push only to your own fork)
Use this only if you want to push your work to GitHub for backup/versioning.

One-time setup (fork + clone)

Fork the course repository on GitHub into your own GitHub account.
Clone your fork (not the instructor’s course repository) with submodules.

Replace FORK_URL with your fork’s URL:
git clone --recurse-submodules FORK_URL
cd MATHXXXSpring20YY

Add the instructor’s course repository as upstream so you can pull course updates.

Replace UPSTREAM_URL with the instructor’s course repository URL:
git remote add upstream UPSTREAM_URL
git remote -v


Getting updates from the instructor (sync upstream → your fork)
From inside your cloned fork:
git fetch upstream
git checkout main
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
git submodule update --init --recursive
git push
If the course repository uses a branch other than main (e.g., master), replace main above accordingly.

title: Git setup: clone the course repository and keep it updated
text:
Common issues and fixes

“fatal: not a git repository”
You’re not inside the course repository folder. Change into it:
cd MATHXXXSpring20YY


“Permission denied (publickey)” (SSH)
You’re using an SSH URL but your SSH key isn’t set up for GitHub. Use the HTTPS URL instead, or configure SSH.


Submodule errors after pulling
Re-run the submodule update:
git submodule update --init --recursive


You accidentally cloned without submodules
From inside the course repository:
git submodule update --init --recursive


Avoid updating submodules beyond what the instructor pinned
Students should not run git submodule update --remote unless explicitly instructed.

title: Policies
section: Academic Integrity, Technology, and AI Usage
text:
Academic Integrity, Technology, and AI Usage
You are encouraged to use technology, including AI tools like ChatGPT, to explore ideas and complete assignments or projects, as long as you understand the work and can explain it yourself. On tests and the final exam, no technology or AI will be allowed unless I say otherwise. Always use these tools to support your learning, not to replace it, and give credit if they meaningfully contribute to your work.
Students are expected to uphold the highest standards of honesty in their academic work, in accordance with Illinois Tech’s Code of Academic Honesty.

Permitted Use

Assignments & Projects: You are encouraged to use technology and AI tools to assist in problem-solving, exploring concepts, and checking work.
You must critically evaluate AI-generated content for accuracy, completeness, and clarity.
You are responsible for understanding and being able to explain any work produced with technological assistance.



Prohibited Use

Tests & Final Exam: No technology, AI tools, or external resources may be used unless explicitly allowed by the instructor.
Submitting AI-generated or technological outputs without personal understanding is prohibited and will be treated as a violation.



Citations & Transparency
If you use AI tools, software, or other external resources in a way that significantly shapes your work, you must acknowledge it (e.g., “Approach suggested by ChatGPT”).


Consequences
Violations will be handled according to Illinois Tech’s Code of Academic Honesty.

Brief bio: Fred J. Hickernell is professor of applied mathematics. His research focuses on improving the efficiency of computer simulations and developing justifiable stopping criteria. He has spent most of his career at Hong Kong Baptist University and Illinois Institute of Technology, often in academic administrative roles. He has served on the editorial boards of the Journal of Complexity, Mathematics of Computation, and the SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis. He is a Fellow of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics and the recipient of the 2016 Joseph F. Traub Prize for Achievement in Information-Based Complexity.
Hickernell speaks Cantonese and enjoys Chinese food. He is married with adult children. He enjoys discussing matters of substance. His most important identity is a disciple of Jesus.

title: Assignments
text:
Unless otherwise stated, you may work on assignments individually or in pairs, and your choice may change from one assignment to the next.
For each assignment, I will create a group set in Canvas; you will sign up to form your group.
Only one person per group submits the assignment in Canvas. The submission is automatically shared with all group members.
Grades and feedback are shared with the whole group. By default, all members receive the same grade.
Assignments are due by 11:59 PM Chicago Time on the due date. Canvas displays due dates in your time zone.
Each submission must include all relevant files:

A self-contained, working copy of any code used.
A PDF version of item 1, including the output, plus any analytical work. Legible handwriting and typed work are both acceptable. You may embed analytical work as Markdown in the code.

title: Project Assessment
text:
Use this project assessment page to provide thoughtful, constructive feedback on a MATH 565 presentation. Review these questions while preparing your own project as well as when observing classmates.
The Fall 2026 procedure for submitting completed assessments is TBA. Topic selection and presentation logistics are maintained separately on the Topic Selection & Presentation Scheduling page.

Presenter’s name:
Project title:
Observer’s name:


1. What are the main points of the presentation?
What question was addressed? What was the main claim, result, feature, or conclusion?
 
 



2. What are the strengths and weaknesses of the article or QMCPy feature?
Consider clarity, insight, technical correctness, evidence, assumptions, limitations, and the value of pursuing the work further.
 
 



3. What did the presenter do well?
Consider organization, pacing, explanation of ideas, examples, visuals, and responses to questions.
 
 



4. How might the presenter have done better?
Identify specific changes that would most improve the presentation’s clarity, correctness, or impact.
